alabama.pd_name: Alabama Office of Indigent Defense Services
alabama.bail_note: Alabama law provides four kinds of bail — judicial public bail (release without security), cash bail, property bail, and professional surety bail (Ala. Code § 15-13-111). Most defendants are entitled to bail, but a judge may deny it for capital offenses and certain violent charges after an Aniah's Law hearing.
alabama.diversion_note: Each district attorney may run a pretrial diversion program under Ala. Code §§ 12-17-226 to 12-17-226.18; admission is in the district attorney's discretion, and a person who completes the agreed conditions can have the charge reduced or dismissed.

alaska.bail_note: Alaska's default is release on personal recognizance or an unsecured appearance or performance bond, with the court required to impose the least restrictive conditions that will reasonably assure appearance and safety (AS 12.30.011). A Department of Corrections pretrial services officer assesses each detained defendant's risk before the first court appearance, and cash or secured bail is used only when nonmonetary conditions are not enough.

arizona.pd_name: Maricopa County Office of the Public Defender
arizona.bail_note: Under A.R.S. § 13-3967, a person charged with a bailable offense must be released on personal recognizance or on bail set by a judicial officer, who weighs factors including the victim's views, the nature of the offense, prior serious or violent convictions, and danger to the community. Bail may be denied only for the limited categories in A.R.S. § 13-3961, such as capital offenses and certain serious felonies, when the proof is evident or the presumption great.
arizona.diversion_note: Under A.R.S. § 11-361, a county attorney may divert or defer prosecution of a person accused of a crime, before a guilty plea or trial, through a special supervision program; the county attorney has sole discretion over who is diverted. State guidelines recommend against diverting serious offenses, offenses requiring sex-offender registration, and dangerous crimes against children, and prosecution is suspended while the person completes the program's conditions.

arkansas.bail_note: Under Arkansas Rule of Criminal Procedure 9.2, a judge may set money bail only after finding that no other conditions will reasonably ensure the defendant's appearance in court. If money bail is set, it takes the form of an unsecured bond, a bond with a 10 percent cash deposit (90 percent of the deposit returned if the defendant appears), or a bond secured by full cash, property, or a surety.
arkansas.diversion_note: Under Arkansas's First Offender Act (Ark. Code § 16-93-303), a person with no prior felony conviction who pleads guilty or no contest may be placed on probation without a judgment of guilt, and the case can be dismissed after successful completion. Arkansas also authorizes a separate pre-adjudication probation program for felony cases (Ark. Code §§ 5-4-901–5-4-913) that requires agreement from both the prosecutor and the court.

california.pd_name: Los Angeles County Public Defender's Office
california.bail_note: Cash bail still exists in California — voters rejected SB 10, the law that would have abolished it, in the 2020 Proposition 25 referendum. Under the California Supreme Court's 2021 decision in In re Humphrey, a court may not keep a person jailed before trial solely because they cannot afford bail; it must consider ability to pay and use the least restrictive nonmonetary conditions, and may order detention only on clear and convincing evidence that no condition short of detention will suffice.
california.diversion_note: California offers several pretrial diversion programs: mental health diversion (Penal Code § 1001.36) lets a court suspend prosecution for up to two years of treatment when a diagnosed mental disorder was a significant factor in a misdemeanor or most felony charges, and drug diversion (Penal Code § 1000) covers first-time nonviolent simple drug possession. In each program, charges are dismissed if the person successfully completes the program.

colorado.pd_name: Office of the Colorado State Public Defender
colorado.bail_note: Colorado law presumes every person in custody is eligible for release on bond with the least restrictive conditions consistent with assuring appearance and public safety, and a monetary condition must be reasonable and account for the person's financial condition (C.R.S. § 16-4-103). Courts start with a personal recognizance bond — release on a written promise to appear with no money up front — and move to a secured monetary bond only when less restrictive options will not work.
colorado.diversion_note: Under C.R.S. § 18-1.3-101, a district attorney may suspend prosecution for up to two years (plus up to one more year for unpaid restitution) while the defendant completes a diversion agreement under probation or program supervision. If the defendant successfully completes the agreement, the court dismisses the charges with prejudice, meaning they cannot be refiled.

connecticut.pd_name: Connecticut Division of Public Defender Services
connecticut.bail_note: Connecticut courts must release an arrested person on the first condition sufficient to reasonably ensure appearance: a written promise to appear, a promise with nonfinancial conditions, a bond without surety, or a bond with surety (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 54-64a). For misdemeanors, the court may not impose financial conditions unless the charge is a family violence crime, the defendant requests them, or the court finds a likely risk of nonappearance, obstruction, or danger — and a 10 percent cash option is automatically available for bail of $20,000 or less.
connecticut.diversion_note: Connecticut's Accelerated Rehabilitation program (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 54-56e) is a court-run pretrial diversion program for defendants charged with certain nonserious crimes or motor vehicle violations who have no prior convictions and have not used the program before (no more than twice total). The court supervises the person for up to two years, and successful completion results in dismissal of the charges and erasure of the records.

delaware.bail_note: Delaware law presumes release on nonmonetary conditions; a court may add financial conditions only if nonmonetary conditions cannot reasonably assure appearance, safety, and the integrity of the process, and must then set the lowest amount it deems reasonably necessary after considering the person's financial resources and ability to pay (11 Del. C. § 2105). Bail is a conditions-of-release bond, which may be unsecured, guaranteed by financial terms, or guaranteed by cash only.
delaware.diversion_note: Delaware's First Offenders Controlled Substances Diversion Program (16 Del. C. § 4767) is for a person with no prior drug conviction who is charged with simple possession or consumption of a controlled substance and has not previously received first-offender treatment. At arraignment the person may elect first-offender treatment, entering a guilty plea as a first offender while the court defers judgment and places the person on probation with conditions including community service and drug education.

florida.bail_note: Since January 1, 2024, the Florida Supreme Court adopts a uniform statewide bond schedule each year, and a person may be released on the scheduled bond before a first appearance hearing; only a judge may set, reduce, or otherwise alter bail (Fla. Stat. § 903.011). Certain people — including those arrested for a felony while on pretrial release, probation, or community control, and those arrested three or more times in the prior six months — may not be released until a judge sets bail at a first appearance hearing based on the criteria in § 903.046.
florida.diversion_note: Florida's pretrial intervention program (Fla. Stat. § 948.08) is open to a first offender, or a person with no more than one prior nonviolent misdemeanor conviction, charged with a misdemeanor or third-degree felony, with approval of the program administrator and consent of the victim, the state attorney, and the judge. Charges are held without final disposition while the person completes counseling, education, supervision, or treatment, and successful completion leads to a recommendation that the charges be dismissed.

georgia.bail_note: All misdemeanor defendants in Georgia have a right to pretrial bail or unsecured judicial release, and courts may not impose excessive bail — only the conditions reasonably necessary to ensure court appearances and protect public safety (O.C.G.A. § 17-6-1). A person arrested on a misdemeanor must be brought before a judge for a bail determination within 48 hours of a warrantless arrest or 72 hours of an arrest on a warrant, and a bail schedule may not be used as the sole basis for setting bail.
georgia.diversion_note: Under O.C.G.A. § 15-18-80, the prosecuting attorney for each judicial circuit may create and run a Pretrial Intervention and Diversion Program, and entry is at the prosecutor's discretion under written guidelines considering the offense, prior record, and the victim's response. A person may not be accepted for an offense carrying a mandatory minimum sentence that cannot be suspended, probated, or deferred, and a person who satisfactorily completes the program has the charges dismissed.

hawaii.bail_note: In Hawaii, bail can take the form of release on one's own recognizance, supervised release, conditional release, or unsecured bail, and a defendant is presumed entitled to bail unless the court finds a risk to appearance, public or witness safety, property, or a prior breach of bail conditions.
hawaii.diversion_note: Hawaii's route is deferred acceptance of a guilty or nolo contendere plea under HRS chapter 853, section 853-1: before trial, a defendant who pleads guilty or no contest may ask the court to defer proceedings without entering a judgment of guilt if the court finds the defendant is unlikely to reoffend and the ends of justice do not require immediate punishment. The court sets conditions, and on successful completion it must discharge the defendant and dismiss the charge, with no adjudication of guilt; expungement may be sought at least one year after discharge under HRS 831-3.2. Certain offenses, including killings, serious-injury felonies, and cases involving a firearm, are excluded under HRS 853-4.

idaho.bail_note: In Idaho, a person charged with a non-capital offense must be admitted to bail or released on their own recognizance before a guilty plea or verdict, and bail may be posted as a cash deposit, property bond, or surety bond; the court may not require bail to be posted only in cash.
idaho.diversion_note: Idaho's statutory diversion program is prosecutor-run under Idaho Code sections 19-3508 and 19-3509, and it is written for first-time DUI: the person must have no commercial license, no injury to another person, and no DUI conviction or prior diversion in the past 10 years. The prosecutor may refer the defendant within 30 days of the citation or charge, and the written agreement lasts at least 12 months and requires an ignition interlock, drug testing, at least 32 hours of community service, and at least 24 hours of drug and alcohol counseling or education. If the defendant completes the agreement, the prosecutor moves to dismiss the case.

illinois.pd_name: Office of the State Appellate Defender
illinois.bail_note: Illinois abolished cash bail under the Pretrial Fairness Act, effective September 18, 2023; release is now decided on an in-or-out basis, with a judge deciding release or detention, generally within 48 hours of arrest, based on risk rather than ability to pay.
illinois.diversion_note: The Cook County State's Attorney's Deferred Prosecution Program offers first-time, non-violent offenders a 12-month program, and a newer Misdemeanor Deferred Prosecution Program refers low-level, nonviolent misdemeanor cases to diversion tracks; successful completion can lead to dismissal and avoidance of a conviction.

indiana.bail_note: Under Indiana Criminal Rule 26, if an arrestee does not present a substantial risk of flight or danger, the court should release the arrestee without money bail or surety, using an evidence-based risk assessment; if money bail is set, it may be satisfied by surety bond, cash deposit, or a 10 percent cash deposit.
indiana.diversion_note: Under Indiana Code 33-39-1-8, a prosecuting attorney may withhold prosecution for a misdemeanor, Level 6 felony, or Level 5 felony if the person agrees to pretrial diversion conditions in a signed agreement filed with the court; murder and Level 1-4 felonies are excluded, and successful completion can lead to dismissal.

iowa.pd_name: Office of the State Public Defender
iowa.bail_note: Under Iowa Code 811.2, all bailable defendants shall be ordered released on personal recognizance or an unsecured appearance bond unless the magistrate finds that release will not reasonably assure appearance or will jeopardize another person's safety, in which case the least restrictive conditions, including a cash deposit of up to 10 percent of the bond, may be imposed.
iowa.diversion_note: Iowa has no statewide pretrial diversion statute, so pretrial diversion is offered locally by individual county attorneys on a case-by-case basis (for example, county marijuana-diversion programs for first-time offenders). Iowa's statewide deferred route is deferred judgment under Iowa Code section 907.3: after a guilty plea or verdict, the court may defer judgment and place the defendant on probation, and on fulfillment of the conditions the defendant is discharged without entry of judgment. Deferred judgment is barred for a prior felony conviction, two or more prior deferred judgments, a forcible felony, and other listed offenses.

kansas.pd_name: Kansas State Board of Indigents' Defense Services
kansas.bail_note: Under K.S.A. 22-2802, a person charged with a crime shall, at first appearance, be ordered released pending trial on an appearance bond in an amount sufficient to assure appearance and public safety, and the magistrate may add conditions such as supervision, travel restrictions, or house arrest.
kansas.diversion_note: Kansas allows pretrial diversion by agreement under K.S.A. 22-2907 through 22-2909: after a complaint is filed and before conviction, the district attorney may propose a diversion agreement if, after weighing the factors in K.S.A. 22-2908, diversion appears to be in the interests of justice and of benefit to the defendant and the community. Each district attorney must adopt written diversion policies and guidelines, and the agreement sets the terms and stays the criminal proceedings; successful completion results in dismissal of the charges. Diversion is barred for some offenses, including a repeat DUI diversion or a DUI involving injury or death.

kentucky.bail_note: Under KRS 431.066, the court considers a pretrial risk assessment and flight and danger risk; a verified, eligible low-risk defendant shall be released on unsecured bond or on their own recognizance, and a defendant generally earns a $100-per-day credit toward bail for each day in jail before trial.
kentucky.diversion_note: Kentucky runs a pretrial diversion program in every judicial circuit under KRS 533.250, aimed mainly at Class D felonies and other offenses for which probation is not barred. A person is eligible if they have had no felony conviction, felony probation or parole, or release from a felony sentence in the 10 years before the offense, have not used diversion in the past five years, and have not committed a sex crime as defined in KRS 17.500. The defendant must enter a guilty or Alford plea, and the court may then postpone imposition of sentence for up to five years on conditions set by the court; successful completion leads to dismissal.
kentucky.legal_aid_name: Kentucky Justice Online (Legal Aid Network of Kentucky)

louisiana.pd_name: Louisiana Office of the State Public Defender
louisiana.bail_note: Under Louisiana Code of Criminal Procedure Article 312, a person in custody charged with an offense is entitled to bail before conviction, except as provided in Articles 312, 312.1, 313, or 313.1, and the amount is set under Article 316 based on appearance, safety, and other statutory factors.
louisiana.diversion_note: Louisiana has no single statewide pretrial diversion statute; district attorneys run their own local diversion programs, and the statewide deferred route is post-conviction. Under Code of Criminal Procedure Article 893(E), after a first-offense noncapital felony conviction the court may defer imposition of sentence and place the defendant on probation, and on satisfactory completion it may set aside the conviction and dismiss the prosecution (no more than twice per person). Article 894 provides a similar deferred-sentence and dismissal route for misdemeanors.

maine.pd_name: Maine Commission on Public Defense Services
maine.bail_note: Under Maine Revised Statutes Title 15, section 1026, a judicial officer shall order pretrial release on personal recognizance or an unsecured appearance bond unless that will not reasonably ensure appearance, refraining from new criminal conduct, integrity of the judicial process, or community safety, in which case the least restrictive further conditions apply.
maine.diversion_note: Maine's route is deferred disposition under 17-A M.R.S. sections 1901 to 1904 (formerly section 1348, repealed in the 2019 sentencing reorganization). A person who has pleaded guilty to a Class B drug crime under chapter 45 or a Class C, D, or E crime and who consents in writing is eligible. The court defers sentencing to a set date and imposes conditions, including refraining from criminal conduct, and at the end of the deferment the prosecutor may move to let the defendant withdraw the guilty plea, after which the charge must be dismissed with prejudice.

maryland.pd_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
maryland.bail_note: Under Maryland Rule 4-216.1, a judicial officer must impose the least onerous release conditions reasonably needed to assure appearance and safety, and must not detain a defendant solely because they cannot afford money bail; a commissioner first sets conditions, followed by a District Court judge's bail review, usually within 24 hours.
maryland.diversion_note: Maryland has no statewide pretrial diversion statute; diversion is run locally by each county State's Attorney's office for first-time, low-level misdemeanors, with the State's Attorney deciding who is referred. The statewide deferred route is probation before judgment under Criminal Procedure section 6-220: after a guilty or nolo contendere plea, or a finding of guilt, the court may stay entry of judgment, defer proceedings, and place the defendant on probation if that serves the best interests of the defendant and the public and the defendant consents in writing. A not-guilty plea variant is also available with the State's consent, where the court finds facts justifying guilt but defers any conviction; successful completion ends the case without a judgment of conviction.

massachusetts.bail_note: Massachusetts starts from release on personal recognizance: a bail magistrate or judge must release a person on their promise to appear unless that will not reasonably assure appearance, and any cash bail must be no higher than needed after considering the person's financial resources (G.L. c. 276, § 58). A person arrested when courts are closed can ask police to call a bail magistrate for release that same night.
massachusetts.diversion_note: Diversion in Massachusetts is run county by county by district attorneys: for example, the Essex County District Attorney offers diversion to first-time, non-violent offenders under 21 and drug treatment on demand for drug-addicted offenders of any age, and successful completion results in dismissal of the criminal complaint.

michigan.bail_note: Michigan courts must release a defendant on personal recognizance or an unsecured appearance bond unless the court finds that will not reasonably ensure appearance or public safety (MCR 6.106(C)); money bail is allowed only after the court states on the record why appearance or safety cannot otherwise be assured, and it can be cash, a surety bond, or a 10% deposit.
michigan.diversion_note: Michigan prosecutors can agree to place a defendant in a pretrial diversion program, and before finalizing a diversion agreement the prosecutor must offer the crime victim a chance to consult about the disposition, including pretrial diversion (MCL 780.756(3)).

minnesota.bail_note: Under Minn. R. Crim. P. 6.02, a person must be released on personal recognizance or an unsecured appearance bond unless the court finds release would endanger public safety or not reasonably assure appearance; if conditions are needed, the court must use the least restrictive one, and must also set a money-only bail option.
minnesota.diversion_note: Under Minn. Stat. § 401.065, every county attorney in a county participating in the Community Corrections Act must run a pretrial diversion program for adult offenders, designed as an alternative to confinement and a criminal conviction; a person who has already completed a Minnesota pretrial diversion program as an adult generally cannot do so again.

mississippi.bail_note: Under Mississippi Code section 99-5-11, a judge or other conservator of the peace may take a recognizance or bond for a person charged with a non-capital offense for which bail is allowed, and may release a misdemeanor defendant on their own recognizance. Financial conditions of bail must not be set for the sole purpose of detaining the defendant, the amount is presumed necessary to assure safety and appearance and presumed attainable, and a defendant who cannot afford it may move to reduce or set aside the bail, which the court must rule on within 48 hours. No misdemeanor defendant may be incarcerated solely because the defendant cannot afford to post bail.
mississippi.diversion_note: Under the Pretrial Intervention Act (Miss. Code § 99-15-105), each district attorney, with a circuit court judge's consent, may establish a pretrial intervention program run under the district attorney's supervision; the program lasts up to three years, and successful completion leads to a noncriminal disposition.

missouri.bail_note: Under Missouri Supreme Court Rule 33.01, a defendant charged with a bailable offense is entitled to release, starting with release on their own recognizance; the court must impose the least restrictive conditions, consider non-monetary conditions first, and may set a monetary condition only after considering the defendant's ability to pay.
missouri.diversion_note: Under RSMo § 557.014, each prosecuting attorney may divert a criminal case to a prosecution diversion program for six months to two years, for nonviolent, nonsexual offenses that do not involve a child victim or an unlawful weapon; the accused must agree to the plan's conditions, and the prosecutor decides who is offered diversion.

montana.bail_note: Under Montana Code Annotated Title 46, chapter 9, the court decides release or detention at the defendant's initial appearance, weighing the nature of the offense, the defendant's history, character, ties, and financial resources, and public safety, and must impose the least restrictive condition or combination of conditions that will ensure appearance and safety (MCA sections 46-9-108 and 46-9-109). When bail is required it must be reasonable in amount and sufficient to ensure the defendant's presence (section 46-9-301). A judge may also set a bail schedule a peace officer can accept, but a person charged with partner or family assault, stalking, violating a protection order, or violating a no-contact order must first appear before a judge (section 46-9-302).
montana.diversion_note: Under MCA § 46-16-130, a prosecutor and a defendant (with counsel or after waiving counsel) may agree in writing to defer prosecution for a set period on conditions such as no new offenses, treatment or counseling, or restitution; if the terms are met, the prosecution is automatically dismissed with prejudice. DUI and aggravated DUI prosecutions cannot be deferred.

nebraska.bail_note: Under Nebraska Revised Statutes section 29-901, any bailable defendant must be ordered released on personal recognizance unless the judge finds that release will not reasonably assure appearance or could jeopardize the safety of victims, witnesses, or others or the maintenance of evidence. For Class IIIA, IV, or V misdemeanors and city or county ordinance violations, release must be on personal recognizance or under other non-monetary conditions unless an exception applies, such as a recent failure to appear. If the judge does require money, the court must consider the defendant's financial ability and impose the least onerous condition that will assure appearance and safety, including a cash deposit of no more than 10 percent of the bond.
nebraska.diversion_note: Under Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 29-3601 to 29-3603, a county attorney may establish a pretrial diversion program with the county board's concurrence; participation is voluntary, the accused has access to counsel before deciding, and successful completion results in dismissal of the charges. Enrollment cannot be conditioned on a guilty plea.

nevada.pd_name: Office of the Nevada State Public Defender
nevada.bail_note: Under Nevada Revised Statutes section 178.484, a person arrested for an offense other than murder of the first degree must be admitted to bail, and a person arrested for first-degree murder may be admitted to bail unless the proof is evident or the presumption great. A court must hold a pretrial release hearing within 48 hours after a person is taken into custody under NRS 178.4849. Under NRS 178.4851, the court may release a person without bail on conditions, and may impose bail or conditions only as the least restrictive means necessary to protect the safety of the community or to ensure the person will appear, considering the factors in NRS 178.4853 and 178.498.
nevada.diversion_note: Under NRS 174.031-174.033, a justice court or municipal court may assign an eligible first-time misdemeanor defendant to a preprosecution diversion program before a plea is entered; successful completion means the court must discharge the defendant and dismiss the charge, with no adjudication of guilt.

new hampshire.bail_note: Under New Hampshire RSA chapter 597, all persons arrested for an offense are eligible for release pending judicial proceedings, except for offenses punishable by death or life without parole, offenses punishable by up to life where the proof is evident or the presumption great, and certain probationers and parolees (RSA 597:1, 597:1-a, 597:1-c, and 597:1-d). Under RSA 597:2, the court must order the person released on personal recognizance or an unsecured appearance bond, released on conditions, detained, or temporarily detained to permit revocation of conditional release. Release on personal recognizance is the default unless the court determines it will not reasonably assure appearance or will endanger the person or the community.
new hampshire.diversion_note: New Hampshire has no single statewide diversion statute; pretrial diversion is run county by county through county attorneys — for example, Strafford County's program, run with the County Attorney's Office, is for people with no prior criminal dealings who the County Attorney does not expect to return to the system. Ask the county attorney's office whether diversion is available in the county where the case is charged.

new jersey.pd_name: New Jersey Office of the Public Defender
new jersey.bail_note: Since January 1, 2017, New Jersey has largely replaced cash bail with a risk-based system: most defendants are released on their own recognizance or with non-monetary conditions and pretrial services monitoring, while prosecutors can ask a judge to detain someone who poses a substantial risk of danger or flight; a judge may still set monetary bail but not to keep someone in jail.
new jersey.diversion_note: New Jersey's Pretrial Intervention (PTI) program, under N.J.S.A. 2C:43-12 and Court Rule 3:28, lets eligible first-time offenders — generally those charged with third- or fourth-degree crimes with no prior diversion — postpone prosecution for up to 36 months of supervision; successful completion results in dismissal of the charges. Apply as early as possible, and no later than 28 days after indictment.

new mexico.pd_name: Law Offices of the Public Defender
new mexico.bail_note: Under the 2016 voter-approved amendment to N.M. Const. art. II, § 13, no one may be held before trial solely because they cannot afford a bond; the default is release on personal recognizance or an unsecured appearance bond, with secured bond only on written findings (N.M. Rule 8-401). Prosecutors can ask a district judge to hold a felony defendant with no bail at all if clear and convincing evidence shows no release conditions will protect the public.
new mexico.diversion_note: New Mexico's Preprosecution Diversion Act (NMSA 1978, §§ 31-16A-1 to -8) requires each district attorney to run a pre-prosecution diversion program. A defendant with no prior violent felony conviction charged with a non-violent offense may be diverted for 6 to 24 months; successful completion means the case is not prosecuted.

new york.pd_name: New York State Office of Indigent Legal Services (state oversight agency; public defense itself is county-based, delivered by county public defender offices, legal aid societies, and assigned counsel programs)
new york.bail_note: Under the 2019 bail reform law (CPL § 510.10, as amended 2020, 2022, and 2023), judges may not set cash bail for most misdemeanors and non-violent felonies and must release the defendant on recognizance or under non-monetary conditions. Cash bail is available only for 'qualifying offenses' (mostly violent felonies and certain sex, domestic-violence, and repeat offenses), and judges may consider only risk of flight, not dangerousness.
new york.diversion_note: New York has no single statewide diversion program. The main route is an adjournment in contemplation of dismissal (ACD) under CPL § 170.55 (local courts) or § 210.47 (superior courts): the case is adjourned for six months (one year for family offenses) and then dismissed and sealed if the defendant stays out of trouble. Judicial Diversion under CPL Article 216 offers court-supervised drug treatment for eligible felony drug cases, and district attorneys run local diversion programs that vary by county.

north carolina.bail_note: Under N.C.G.S. Chapter 15A, Article 26, every defendant charged with a noncapital offense has a statutory right to pretrial release, and the court must impose the least restrictive conditions that will reasonably assure appearance. Release can be on an unsecured bond, in the custody of a designated person or organization, on a secured bond (cash deposit, mortgage, or surety), or on house arrest with electronic monitoring; each judicial district publishes its own pretrial release policies.
north carolina.diversion_note: Deferred prosecution under N.C.G.S. § 15A-1341(a1) lets a prosecutor, with court approval, defer prosecution of a Class H or I felony or a misdemeanor by written agreement and place the defendant on probation (up to two years) to demonstrate good conduct; successful completion leads to dismissal. Conditional discharge under § 15A-1341(a4) works similarly after a guilty plea or finding, without entering a judgment of guilt.
sources: https://www.NCcourts.gov/assets/documents/local-rules-forms/Amended Official Policies on Pretrial Release- Remediated.pdf

north dakota.pd_name: North Dakota Commission on Legal Counsel for Indigents
north dakota.bail_note: Under N.D.R.Crim.P. 46, a magistrate must order release on a written promise to appear or an unsecured bond unless that will not reasonably assure the defendant's return to court. Only then may the court set a secured amount or add conditions such as no-contact orders, travel limits, or check-ins; the statutory framework is in N.D.C.C. Chapter 29-08.
north dakota.diversion_note: House Bill 1425 (2025) authorizes each county state's attorney to create a prosecution-led diversion program: with court approval, the prosecutor and defendant may agree to suspend prosecution, and the case is dismissed under N.D.R.Crim.P. 32.2 if the defendant commits no new offense during the agreement period. Each county that establishes a program must adopt written guidelines and minimum eligibility criteria.

ohio.pd_name: Office of the Ohio Public Defender
ohio.bail_note: Under Ohio Rev. Code § 2937.011, a court must release a defendant on the least restrictive conditions that will reasonably assure appearance, public safety, and no obstruction of the process, and any financial conditions must be the least costly to the defendant while still assuring appearance. Bail can be an unsecured bond, a 10% cash deposit, or a surety bond, and a person who is arrested must get an initial bail hearing no later than the second court day after arrest.
ohio.diversion_note: Ohio courts may require participation in a diversion program as a condition of pretrial release (ORC § 2937.011(D)(8)). Ask the prosecutor or the court whether a pretrial diversion option is available for the specific charge, since programs and eligibility vary by county and prosecutor.

oklahoma.bail_note: Under Oklahoma's Pretrial Release Act (22 O.S. § 1105.2), bail is set by the court after arrest, the court must set the least restrictive conditions necessary to reasonably assure appearance, and a bond hearing must occur within 48 hours of arrest. A defendant who cannot obtain a surety or deposit the bond amount may be released on an own-recognizance bond (except for listed offenses), and larger counties may operate pretrial release programs that evaluate defendants and supervise release.
oklahoma.diversion_note: Oklahoma has two deferred tracks. Under 22 O.S. § 305.1, a district attorney may agree not to file charges for up to three years under a written deferred prosecution agreement with conditions, and each DA's office must adopt guidelines weighing factors such as the evidence, whether the offense was nonviolent, and the victim's views. Under 22 O.S. § 991c, a court may also defer sentence after a guilty or no-contest plea without entering a judgment of guilt, dismissing the case if all conditions are completed.

oregon.pd_name: Oregon Public Defense Commission (formerly the Office of Public Defense Services)
oregon.bail_note: Under SB 48 (2021), ORS 135.230 to 135.290, a magistrate must first consider release on personal recognizance, then conditional release, and only then security release, and must set the lowest security amount that will reasonably assure appearance. There is no fixed bail schedule: release follows the Chief Justice's statewide guidelines and each judicial district's standing pretrial release order, and when security is set the deposit is usually 10% of the amount (minimum $25).
oregon.diversion_note: Oregon's main diversion route is the DUII diversion program under ORS 813.200: an eligible first-time DUII defendant may petition within 30 days of first appearance, and if the court accepts the agreement and the defendant completes treatment and other conditions over one year, the charge is dismissed. General diversion is also authorized under ORS 135.881 to 135.901, with eligibility and terms set by the local district attorney.

pennsylvania.pd_name: County public defender offices (Pennsylvania has no statewide public defender office; state funding and standards are handled through the Pennsylvania Commission on Crime and Delinquency's Indigent Defense Advisory Committee)
pennsylvania.bail_note: Under Pa.R.Crim.P. 524, there are five types of release on bail: release on recognizance, release on nonmonetary conditions, an unsecured bail bond, nominal bail (such as $1), and release on a monetary condition. The judge must consider release on recognizance first, and any monetary condition must be no greater than necessary to reasonably assure appearance and compliance; a deposit of up to 10% of the amount may be allowed.
pennsylvania.diversion_note: Pennsylvania's Accelerated Rehabilitative Disposition (ARD) program (Pa.R.Crim.P. 310-320) is a pretrial diversion program for first-time, non-violent offenders. Admission is entirely at the district attorney's discretion; participants complete supervision, community service, and program costs, and on successful completion the charges are dismissed and the defendant may seek expungement.

rhode island.pd_name: Rhode Island Office of the Public Defender
rhode island.bail_note: Under R.I.G.L. § 12-13-1.3, pretrial release means release without bail on non-monetary conditions set by the court, and there is a presumption of release on personal recognizance. The only monetary conditions allowed are giving surety or depositing 10% of the bail amount (§ 12-13-10); cash-only bail is barred except in cases where the defendant owes court-ordered restitution.
rhode island.diversion_note: Rhode Island runs an Adult Diversion Program through the Attorney General's Office (established 1976) for first-time, non-violent felony offenders, and a Superior Court Diversion Program under R.I.G.L. § 8-2-39.3 for eligible felony and certain misdemeanor defendants. Both offer supervision and services instead of conviction, and successful completion leads to dismissal of the charge.

south carolina.pd_name: South Carolina Commission on Indigent Defense
south carolina.bail_note: Under S.C. Code § 22-5-510, a person charged with a bailable offense must have a bond hearing within 24 hours of arrest. Under § 17-15-10, release on a personal recognizance bond is the default for noncapital offenses unless the court finds it will not reasonably assure appearance or would create an unreasonable danger; otherwise the court may require a surety bond, a cash bond, or a cash deposit of up to 10% of the bond.
south carolina.diversion_note: South Carolina's Pretrial Intervention (PTI) program, under S.C. Code §§ 17-22-10 to -170, is run by the solicitor in each judicial circuit for first-time, non-violent offenders with no significant criminal history. It typically lasts 90 days to one year and requires community service, counseling, restitution, and fees (a $100 application fee and $250 participation fee); successful completion means the charge is dismissed and the arrest record can be expunged. DUI and crimes of violence are excluded.

south dakota.pd_name: Office of Indigent Legal Services (overseen by the Commission on Indigent Legal Services)
south dakota.bail_note: South Dakota law starts with release on personal recognizance (a signed promise to appear) and only adds cash or other conditions if that will not reasonably assure appearance (SDCL 23A-43-2 and 23A-43-3); an appearance bond can be satisfied by depositing up to 10 percent of the bond amount in cash with the court clerk. Almost everyone is entitled to bail except in capital cases with strong proof of guilt.
south dakota.diversion_note: South Dakota law allows each state's attorney to create a deferred prosecution program for general misdemeanor offenses other than driving while intoxicated. The state's attorney decides whether a case is appropriate, mails the defendant notice of the alleged offense and the proposed restitution or community service, and may enter a written agreement deferring prosecution for up to 180 days while the defendant completes the agreed community service, restitution, and costs. A fee of no more than $50 may be charged if the state's attorney's office administers the case, and successful completion means the defendant is not prosecuted for the offense in the agreement.

tennessee.bail_note: Tennessee's constitution makes all prisoners bailable except in capital cases where the proof is evident, and state law (Tenn. Code Ann. 40-11-115) requires the magistrate to consider release on personal recognizance or an unsecured bond first and impose the least restrictive conditions that will reasonably ensure appearance and community safety.
tennessee.diversion_note: Tennessee pretrial diversion, governed by TCA 40-15-105 and also called suspended prosecution, is available only to a narrow class of qualified defendants: the defendant must not have previously received pretrial or judicial diversion, must not have a disqualifying prior conviction, and must not be charged with a felony or certain excluded misdemeanors such as DUI or a sex offense. The defendant enters a memorandum of understanding with the district attorney, prosecution is suspended for up to two years while the defendant meets its terms, and if the terms are not met prosecution resumes; on successful completion the defendant may ask the court for an order of expungement.
tennessee.legal_aid_name: Legal Aid Society of Middle Tennessee and the Cumberlands

texas.bail_note: Texas has no statewide public defender office; each county appoints counsel under the Fair Defense Act, overseen by the Texas Indigent Defense Commission. Under Senate Bill 9 (2025), a person charged with a felony must appear before a magistrate who considers a public safety report before bail is set, and personal (no-cash) bonds are barred for a longer list of offenses, including unlawful possession of a firearm and violation of a family-violence protective order.
texas.diversion_note: Texas prosecutors operate pretrial intervention programs, and Senate Bill 9 (2025) requires the state to enter the conditions of a defendant's pretrial intervention program into the statewide law-enforcement database within 10 business days of the defendant entering the program.

utah.bail_note: Utah judges may release a defendant on personal recognizance, an unsecured bond, cash bail, or a commercial surety bond, and must impose only conditions that are reasonably available and necessary to ensure appearance and safety; when a financial condition is imposed, the judge must consider the person's ability to pay (Utah Code 77-20-205). Bail amounts start from a statewide financial-condition schedule tied to the offense class.
utah.diversion_note: Utah's route is a plea in abeyance under Utah Code Title 77, chapter 2a, section 77-2a-3: with the consent of both the prosecuting attorney and the defendant, the court accepts a plea but holds it in abeyance under an agreement that may require a fee, restitution, treatment, and other probation-like conditions. On successful completion the court may reduce the degree of the offense, allow the defendant to withdraw the plea and dismiss the case, or, after a certified problem-solving court program, order expungement. A plea may not be held in abeyance without the prosecutor's consent.

vermont.bail_note: Vermont law presumes release on personal recognizance or an unsecured appearance bond, and cash bail may be used only to address flight risk, not to punish (13 V.S.A. 7554). No bail, secured bond, or appearance bond may be imposed at the initial appearance for a cited misdemeanor, and bail for a misdemeanor eligible for sealing is capped at $200.
vermont.diversion_note: Vermont runs a statewide adult court diversion program administered by the Attorney General under 3 V.S.A. section 164, available in all counties for both pre-charge and post-charge referrals. Post-charge diversion is for people charged with a first or second misdemeanor or a first nonviolent felony, or other offenses the prosecutor deems appropriate, and for people with substance-use or mental-health treatment needs regardless of criminal history (except listed felonies). It is a restorative program in which the person takes responsibility and works to repair the harm, and the prosecutor dismisses the charge of a person who successfully completes it.

virginia.bail_note: Under Virginia Code 19.2-123, a judicial officer may release an arrested person on a promise to appear, an unsecured bond, a secured bond (surety or cash deposit), or under pretrial-services supervision, with conditions such as no contact with the victim, curfew, or drug testing. A person arrested for a felony who has a prior felony conviction, is already on bond, or is on probation or parole may be released only on a secured bond.
virginia.diversion_note: Virginia has no general statewide pretrial diversion program; instead it uses deferred disposition, which requires the agreement of both the defendant and the prosecutor under Virginia Code section 19.2-298.02. A dedicated first-offender route exists under section 19.2-303.2 for certain misdemeanor property crimes: a person with no prior felony conviction and no prior dismissal under that section may have proceedings deferred without entry of a judgment of guilt and be placed on probation, including restitution, and on fulfillment of the terms the court discharges the person and dismisses the proceedings without an adjudication of guilt.

washington.pd_name: Washington State Office of Public Defense
washington.bail_note: Washington court rule CrR 3.2 presumes release on personal recognizance in noncapital cases; the court may impose conditions, including monetary conditions, only after finding that recognizance will not reasonably assure appearance or that the person is likely to commit a violent crime or intimidate witnesses. If no probable cause is found, the person must be released without conditions.
washington.diversion_note: Washington's route is deferred prosecution under RCW chapter 10.05, available in a court of limited jurisdiction to a person charged with a misdemeanor or gross misdemeanor. The person must petition at least seven days before trial and allege under oath that the conduct was caused by a substance-use disorder, mental-health disorder, or domestic-violence behavior problem needing treatment, with a case history and assessment from an approved provider, and the court must make the findings required by RCW 10.05.020. If the court approves a treatment plan and the person completes it, the charges are dismissed under RCW 10.05.120; a second deferred prosecution for DUI is allowed only on the terms of RCW 10.05.010.

west virginia.bail_note: Under West Virginia Code 62-1C-1a, a person charged with a misdemeanor must be released on personal recognizance at first appearance unless charged with a listed offense (such as a violent misdemeanor, a drug offense, or one involving a minor victim); for all other jailable offenses the person is entitled to bail under the least restrictive conditions reasonably necessary to assure appearance and safety.
west virginia.diversion_note: West Virginia allows a prosecuting attorney to enter a written pretrial diversion agreement under W. Va. Code section 61-11-22 when the prosecutor considers it in the interests of justice. The agreement lasts no more than 24 months, its terms may be similar to probation conditions, and a person who successfully complies is not subject to prosecution for the offense or offenses set out in the agreement. Separately, section 61-11-22a provides deferred adjudication, in which the court may defer acceptance of a guilty plea and further adjudication on terms set by the court.

wisconsin.bail_note: Under Wisconsin Statutes 969.02, a judge may release a person charged with a misdemeanor without bail or on an unsecured appearance bond, or may require a surety bond or cash deposit instead; a signature bond means release with no money paid up front, while a cash bond must be paid before release. Wisconsin does not use commercial bail bondsmen.
wisconsin.diversion_note: Wisconsin uses deferred prosecution agreements under Wis. Stat. sections 971.37 to 971.39, run by the district attorney. Under section 971.37, for domestic-abuse crimes, and section 971.39, in counties under 100,000 people, the district attorney, the department, and the defendant may enter a written agreement under which the defendant admits the elements of the crime and meets conditions such as treatment or programs, with the department monitoring compliance. If the agreement is completed, the court dismisses the charges with prejudice; if it is terminated or the defendant fails to comply, prosecution may resume. The district attorney may also require community service as a condition under section 971.38.

wyoming.pd_name: Office of the State Public Defender
wyoming.bail_note: Wyoming's constitution makes all non-capital defendants bailable, and court rule 46.1 requires a judge to release a defendant on an unsecured bond unless that will not reasonably assure appearance, weighing the nature of the offense, the evidence, family and community ties, and any danger to others. Release can also be on recognizance or a cash or surety bond, with conditions such as no contact with an alleged victim.
wyoming.diversion_note: Wyoming's first-offender deferred route is Wyo. Stat. section 7-13-301: a person with no prior felony conviction who is charged with, found guilty of, or pleads guilty or no contest to a qualifying misdemeanor or felony (excluding murder, first- or second-degree sexual assault, aggravated assault and battery, and first- or second-degree arson) may, with the consent of the defendant and the state, have proceedings deferred without entry of a judgment of guilt and be placed on probation on court-set terms. If the court finds the terms fulfilled and rehabilitation attained, it may discharge the person and dismiss the proceedings without an adjudication of guilt; only one discharge and dismissal under this section is allowed.
